sections.title: A New Creation and a Dwelling with God

blocks.text: Revelation 21 presents the end of the story as a new heaven and new earth, with the old order passed away. New Jerusalem descends from God, God dwells with humanity, and death, mourning, crying, and pain are said to be no more. The chapter's images therefore move from cosmic renewal to a city whose life is defined by divine presence. This is the chapter's promised new creation, not simply an improved version of the present order.

Jerusalem was a royal and cultic center where kingship, worship, pilgrimage, and imperial pressure met. It gathered Israel's memory around chosen place, Davidic rule, temple presence, judgment, and hope for restored worship. Revelation's New Jerusalem reuses city and temple imagery familiar in the ancient world, but the vision transforms that imagery around God's direct presence.

The name Jerusalem carries a long story: it moves from a Jebusite city to Davidic capital and temple center, then becomes a focal point of exile, return, and messianic expectation. Against that background, New Jerusalem appears as the final hope of the biblical story, reshaping Zion imagery after judgment and exile.

In the ancient Near East, temples were understood as divine dwellings and royal-cultic centers. Israel's temple was distinguished by covenant holiness and the Lord's chosen presence. The temple symbol joined sacred space with holiness, sacrifice, priesthood, purity, mediation, and pilgrimage; in the Second Temple period it also shaped worship, national hope, and conflicts over authority. That background helps a reader hear the force of the vision's claim that the city has no separate temple building.

Temple imagery develops through a sequence: God's tabernacle presence in the wilderness, Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, the temple's judgment and destruction, restored worship, and later rereading of sacred space in the New Testament. Revelation 21 carries that sequence into New Jerusalem. The city has no temple because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, so the divine presence that temples signified is no longer represented by a separate building.

The chapter shares dwelling and holiness language with other sanctuary passages, but those passages should not be flattened into one referent. Tabernacle, First Temple, Second Temple, Christological and community metaphors, heavenly sanctuary, and new creation remain distinct ways the material is presented. This distinction also matters ethically: later Christian sanctuary readings cannot be used to authorize antisemitism, replacement claims, seizure or destruction of holy places, or immunity from accountability.

The city vision continues into Revelation 22:1-5. Across this larger sequence, New Jerusalem combines city, bride, sanctuary, Eden, and renewed-Zion imagery. Revelation repeatedly reworks Israel's Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. Its sequence particularly recomposes Ezekielian images of the throne, creature, scroll, measuring, witness, plague, Gog, battle, city, river, and tree.
